Mekonah
meh-KOH-nah
n. (a town of Judah resettled after the Babylonian captivity, named once)
Hebrew Mekonah, a base or a foundation, from the root kun, to establish; named once in Scripture, at Nehemiah 11:28.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Mekonah is a town of the south of Judah, named once, in Nehemiah's roll of the villages reoccupied by the returned captives: “And at Ziklag, and at Mekonah, and in the villages thereof” (Nehemiah 11:28). The name means a base or a foundation, from the verb to establish, and no name could suit the chapter better. Nehemiah 11 is the record of a people being set back upon their foundations. The holy city had to be repopulated by lot, because men would not willingly leave their fields for a ruined capital: “And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities” (Nehemiah 11:1). The remaining nine parts went out to places like Mekonah, and the chapter names them one after another — Kirjatharba, Dibon, Jekabzeel (Nehemiah 11:25), then Zanoah and Adullam and Lachish and Azekah, “And they dwelt from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom” (Nehemiah 11:30). The restoration was not a single dramatic act but the slow reoccupation of a hundred small foundations. That is how God generally restores a people: village by village, by the plain obedience of men who went where the lot sent them.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Mekonah is a biblical place-name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Mekonah is the name of a town in the south of Judah; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

It occurs once in the Authorized Version, at Nehemiah 11:28.

The Hebrew name means a base or a foundation.

It is from the root kun, to establish or to set firm.

It appears in the roll of villages reoccupied after the Babylonian captivity.

Key Scripture

Neh 11:28 — "And at Ziklag, and at Mekonah, and in the villages thereof,"

Neh 11:1 — "And the rulers of the people dwelt at Jerusalem: the rest of the people also cast lots, to bring one of ten to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city, and nine parts to dwell in other cities."

Neh 11:25 — "And for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjatharba, and in the villages thereof, and at Dibon, and in the villages thereof, and at Jekabzeel, and in the villages thereof,"

Neh 11:30 — "Zanoah, Adullam, and in their villages, at Lachish, and the fields thereof, at Azekah, and in the villages thereof. And they dwelt from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom."

Modern Corruption

Restoration is imagined as a dramatic event rather than the unglamorous reoccupation of ordinary ground, which is what Nehemiah 11 records.

expand to see more

A people expecting revival to arrive as a single spectacle will not recognise it when it comes as a list of villages. Nehemiah 11 is the shape of real restoration: lots cast, families moved, fields worked again, a hundred small foundations rebuilt by men whose names appear once. The rebuilding of a wall gets the attention; the repopulating of Mekonah is the harder and longer work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God restores His people by ordinary obedience in ordinary places, and that a man sent to a village has been sent by the same hand that assigned the rulers to Jerusalem.
